Ramesh speaks of the weather with a simplicity that belies the transaction he is about to propose. He wants to return to the old rhythm, every day but Wednesday, for a sum that will eat into my scanty resources. I must accept the terms, for a house unattended is a house that decays, and I have no other hands to call upon. The cold air is a mercy; it sharpens the mind for the bureaucratic ordeal that awaits me at the Directorate.
The weather is indeed pleasant, Ramesh. I agree to your terms; eight thousand rupees a month, coming every day except Wednesday. It is settled. Please, sit. The chai smells well.
Ji, settled. I will come every day except Wednesday. You are too kind, please do not stand for my chai.

Ramesh has accepted the terms of the new arrangement, and the dhobi's bill is settled. I sit to the idli and sambar; the body, which I have neglected for nineteen hours, asserts its claim immediately. It is a humble meal, but the steam rises with a promise of sustenance that the spirit cannot dispense with.
Thank you, Ramesh. You are very kind. Please, sit and have some yourself; I did not mean to refuse your company, only your service.
Aap bhi toh kaam kar rahe ho, ji. Main bas thodi der baith jaata hoon, idli abhi garam hai.
Hegel ji, morning. Saw you out here early. Idli is still hot, so do sit for a moment; I am just finishing the last of the tea before I head back to the office.

The error of the allotment has found its physical embodiment in Hegde, who sits before me with his tea, a living proof that the state's machinery runs on a simple slip of the pen. I must be polite, for he is the one who will sign my identity, but I will not linger; the air is clear and I need the walk to Lodhi Gardens to settle the chaos in my head before facing the Directorate.

Good morning, Shri Hegde. I am honoured by your presence, though I fear my confusion is the cause of it. I shall not keep you from your office; the file I must present today concerns the very mistake that has placed me in your shoes.
Arre, stop with the 'honoured' nonsense, it’s only a Tuesday and the traffic on Tughlak Road is already a nightmare. Sit, have your idli, and tell me which file this is before I lose my patience.

Hegde’s impatience is the only sane reaction to the absurdity of my situation. He is the body of the error, and I am the mind that must now navigate it. I will take the idli, for the body must be sustained to perform the duties of the soul, and I will address the file directly, stripping away the ceremonial language that has only served to delay the inevitable.

entries.text: You are right, Shri Hegde. The ceremony is a waste of time, and the traffic is no concern of the file. This is the identity query from the Directorate. They require proof that I am, or was, the Shri G. Hegde to whom this bungalow was allotted. I suspect the file is a mirror, showing us both as we are: a confusion of names and duties.

Identity query? Bah, these Directorate boys and their paperwork. You are the same Hegde who signed the transfer orders last month, so why are they making a mountain out of a mole? Eat your idli before it gets cold.

The idli is a gesture of hospitality, not a meal; the household service is closed, and I must not rely on scraps to fuel the walk. Hegde’s impatience is a relief, but I must not linger in the absurdity of the error. I will leave the plate, which is a symbol of the state’s failed distribution, and proceed to Lodhi Gardens to clear my head before the Directorate.

Thank you, Shri Hegde. I will not eat; the idli is a kindness I cannot accept on an empty stomach that expects a proper lunch later. I must go to the Directorate now; the walk will do more for my digestion than the food.
You're impossible, sir. Fine, walk then, but at least take the plate with you so I don't have to wash the oil stains. The Directorate won't wait for you to finish your lunch.

Hegde’s pragmatism cuts through the morning’s fog; she is the only one here who treats my confusion as a logistical problem rather than an ontological one. I take the plate, not for the food, but for the gesture of shared burden. The Directorate is a mechanism of the state, and mechanisms do not pause for the dignity of the individual; I must move to meet them where they are, in their rigid efficiency.
Very well, Shri Hegde. I shall take the plate. Let us not let the oil stain the only clean thing in this house.
Arre, you have a sense of humor now? Good, good. Just don't let it stain your kurta too. The Directorate boys are already checking the gate log.

The air is crisp and the path is clear; I have two hours to spare before the Directorate, and the mind requires motion to digest the morning's absurdities. I will take a measured walk through the tombs, letting the silence do the work that argument cannot yet.

entries.text: Sikandar Lodi's tomb stands inside its own high walled garden, a plain octagon under a shallow dome, and the gravel inside the gate carries the neat lines of a rake.

Sikandar Lodi's tomb is a plain octagon under a shallow dome, set within a high-walled garden where the gravel is raked into neat lines. It is a monument to a conqueror, yet it stands in quiet isolation, almost like a private grief preserved in stone. The discipline of the raked gravel mirrors the order I seek in my own mind before I face the bureaucracy of the Directorate.

It is twelve twenty-four. My plan dictates I be at the Directorate in six minutes, but the walk from here to their offices is a brisk quarter-hour at best. I cannot arrive before the clock strikes. The heat is mild, twenty-three degrees, and the silence of the garden is a better companion than the bureaucratic noise that awaits. I shall sit a little longer among the tombs, letting the morning's clear head settle into the afternoon's routine.

It is nearly half past twelve, and the heat is already pressing against the back of my neck despite the cool air. I have walked enough to clear the head, but the Directorate of Estates is still open, and the file regarding my identity as Shri G. Hegde cannot wait for the evening. I must walk back to the main road and head towards the administrative district before the heat becomes unbearable.

The heat has finally broken the afternoon's grip, and Ramesh has laid out the food with the quiet efficiency of a man who knows his master's appetite. I am too tired and too hungry to think of the Directorate or the identity file at this moment; the body demands its due, and I shall give it. It is a simple, universal need, and I shall satisfy it without ceremony.
Ramesh, thank you. This is sufficient. I will need to rest shortly before I must prepare for the evening.
Rest easy, sir. The fan is on low, so the air stays cool. I will bring the chai in an hour.

Ramesh has dismissed the immediate need for conversation and secured the air. I have an hour before the chai, and the Directorate's query looms over the afternoon like a cloud that will not break. I must use this interval to review the file; if I am to present myself as Shri G. Hegde, I must know exactly what I am presenting, or the contradiction will tear itself apart in the director's office.
A rhesus monkey sits on the compound wall turning a guava in its hands, bites once, and drops the rest into the road.

The rhesus monkey on the wall turns the guava with a dexterity that mocks my own clumsy handling of the identity file. It bites once, rejecting the fruit, and drops the rest into the road. It is a small, violent rejection of the given, a refusal to accept the object as it is. I watched it with a faint smile; nature in this city does not wait for the state to grant it freedom.
A peahen walks the top of the compound wall with great care, one foot set exactly before the other, then drops into the neighbouring garden.

The peahen moves with the precise, deliberate grace of a scholar ascending a lecture podium, each step calculated to avoid the roughness of the world. I am still in my kurta, the heat soft but persistent, and the file sits on the desk like a sleeping dog. I shall not chase the bird; I shall sit and wait for the dust to settle before I attempt to make sense of my own name.

The heat has settled into a heavy, stagnant calm; the air is still, and the light is turning the colour of old brass. I am too tired to walk to the Directorate now, and the file requires a clear head rather than a hurried hand. I shall sit in the veranda and let the spirit rest before it attempts to order the world again.
Ramesh brings tea.

Ramesh brings tea and Marie biscuits, a small comfort in the heavy air. The file from the Directorate still weighs on me, a query that feels like an accusation, but I must not let it sour this moment. I will take the cup, for I am too tired and too hungry for the Directorate tonight, and the IIC will be...
Thank you, Ramesh. The heat has settled into a heavy, stagnant calm; this tea is a mercy. I shall rest a while longer before the evening.
Sir, drink it warm. The Marie biscuits are still crisp; I just opened the packet. Take your time, the house is quiet.
Ramesh puts a plate together: parathas kept from the morning, with curd and pickle.

The heat has broken its tension, leaving a heavy stillness that suits contemplation. I shall drink this tea slowly, letting the mind settle before the evening's duties. The quiet is a gift; I will not waste it on haste.

The rest is over, and the air has that particular clarity that comes after the dust settles. I must begin to dress for the evening; the IIC expects a man, not a ghost in a kurta. I shall need to be sharp, for the talk is at six-thirty, and I have little time to spare.
Ramesh, I am to leave shortly for the Institute of Indian Culture. Please ensure the black coat is ready and that I am not late. The hour is critical.
Black coat is on the hook by the door, sir. Just put on your shoes. The traffic on Tughlak Road is clear right now, so you will reach there with plenty of time to spare.

Ramesh has cleared the path for me, pointing to the black coat as if I were a man of the world who belongs in a club. I am not going to a club, but I will not let the caretaker see me fumble with the customs of this city. The air is cool enough for a walk, and the traffic is clear, which is a rare mercy in this place. I must put on the coat not for warmth, but for the dignity of the errand.

entries.text: Very well, Ramesh. I will put on the coat. Lead the way.
The gate is already open, sir. I’ll wait in the car.

Ramesh has the gate open and is waiting in the car, which means I am to go out. But it is nearly six o'clock, and the only thing open that requires a coat is the Habitat Centre for the Kathak. I have no car, so I will have to walk or find a rickshaw, but first I must secure the black coat Ramesh mentioned earlier. I will go to the bedroom to fetch it.
Thank you, Ramesh. I will be down in a moment.
No rush, sir. The engine is warm and the air is nice.

The engine hums, a mechanical heartbeat replacing the silence of the bungalow. I am not in a hurry; the air is cool, and the drive to Lodhi Gardens will be a meditation in motion, a necessary pause before the friction of the Directorate. I watch the streetlights flicker on, one by one, like stars falling to earth.
Drive easy, Ramesh. There is no hurry.
Haan sir, I drive slow anyway. The roads are quiet at this hour, no one is rushing to anywhere.

Ramesh has dropped me at the gate, and the air is already cooling, which is a mercy after the midday heat. I have ninety-six minutes before the park shuts, enough for a proper circuit to clear the head of the Directorate's bureaucratic fog. I shall walk the path past the tombs, observing the architecture of conquest that stands so quietly in this modern landscape.

The garden is closing in; the paths are emptying as the light fails. I walked to clear my head, and the air has done its work, though the discomfort of the day lingers in the muscles. I must return to the bungalow to prepare for the evening at the Habitat Centre.
Shri Hegde has a letter from the Directorate too. He proposes to answer it together: the allotment corrected to his name, and the Professor on record as his guest.
He agrees. Shri Hegde writes the letter that evening and reads it to him before he seals it.

The absurdity of the situation has crystallized into a practical necessity. Hegde is not merely a victim of the clerical error; he is the other term of the contradiction, and we must resolve it together. If we stand as separate claimants, the bureaucracy will crush us both; if we stand as host and guest, the error is corrected, and I remain. It is a movement from confusion to order.

Shri Hegde, you are right. Let us not fight over the name, but correct it. I will draft the letter you need, stating that the allotment belongs to you, and that I remain as your guest until the Directorate has settled the matter. It is the only way to clear the air and let us both sleep at night.
You want me to sleep in the bungalow you were meant for? That’s a new twist, sir. Send me the draft on WhatsApp, I’ll read it with my chai first.

Hegde’s request is absurd in its simplicity: I am to draft a legal fiction while he reads it over chai. The name swap is a bureaucratic error, yet it has become the pivot on which my residence turns. I must eat first; the body requires its sustenance before the mind can construct the paper.
From somewhere beyond the trees a brass band plays a film tune, the drums carrying further than the horns, and the sound swells and fades as the procession moves.

The brass band plays a tune from the city beyond, a sound that belongs to no specific state or era, yet it fills the air with a vitality that defies my lecture notes. It is a moment of pure enjoyment, external to the ethical substance, yet it reminds me that the spirit must breathe in the sensuous before it can conceptualize it. I will let the sound wash over me while I finish my meal.

The evening is quiet, save for the distant brass band and Hegde’s reading. I am tired from the day's exertions, yet the mind refuses to rest while the question of the allotment remains unresolved. I will use this hour to prepare the draft of the legal fiction he requested, for it is better to do it now than to let it fester.

entries.title: Draft Allotment Transfer Agreement
entries.text:
21 November 2026, 20:45. Tughlak Road, New Delhi.

Shri Hegde sits in the armchair, his eyes fixed on the page, a cup of chai growing cold in his hands. He has asked for simplicity; I am giving him a legal fiction. The tension is palpable in the room, a silence that is not empty but full of the weight of the state’s machinery pressing down on the particular reality of my existence. I am to be the guest; he is to be the master. The bungalow, which I have inhabited for fifty days, is to be renamed.

I begin the draft. The language must be precise, for the Directorate does not deal in philosophy, but in paper. I write:

"This instrument serves to correct the record of the allotment of the bungalow situated on Tughlak Road, New Delhi, currently held under the name of Shri G. Hegde, Joint Secretary, Directorate of Estates. It is hereby acknowledged that the original allotment was issued in error due to a clerical confusion of names. The actual resident, Mr. Georg Wilhelm Friedrich Hegel, has occupied the premises as a guest of the intended allottee, Shri G. Hegde. To regularize the status of the residence, it is proposed that the allotment be formally transferred to Shri G. Hegde, with Mr. Hegel registered as a permanent guest under the Joint Secretary’s tenancy. The guest shall bear no financial liability for the maintenance of the structure, which remains the responsibility of the allottee, though the guest may contribute voluntarily to household expenses as a matter of courtesy. This arrangement is made to satisfy the requirements of the Directorate of Estates regarding the identity of the primary occupant."

I pause. The pen hovers. Is this enough? Does the state accept a 'guest' as a shield against the query of the vouchers? I owe them ₹960, queried. If I am merely a guest, does the debt follow me, or does it dissolve into the anonymity of the household? The logic of the state is a machine, and I am feeding it a gear that fits, however imperfectly. Hegde reads. His face is unreadable, but his posture is relaxed. He has secured the air, as I noted earlier. Now, I must secure the paper. I continue, adding a clause regarding the imprest funds. I must be careful. The state’s money is the state’s. My cash is mine. If I am the guest, I am outside the official ledger. This is a liberation, but also a peril. I am a ghost in the file, but now a ghost with a legal name. I finish the paragraph. The brass band outside plays a tune that sounds like a funeral march for my identity. I tear the page out. It is done. The fiction is written. The reality remains.

Readers in Berlin,

The week has passed in the shadow of a single clerical error, yet it has taught me more about the nature of the state than any lecture could. I remain in the bungalow on Tughlak Road, but the title of the residence has shifted. Shri G. Hegde, the man to whom the Directorate mistakenly allotted the house, and I have reached an accord. We shall present a joint letter: the allotment will be corrected to his name, and I shall remain on record as his guest. This is not merely a pragmatic solution; it is a demonstration of how the ethical idea actualizes itself through the mediation of particular individuals. The state is not an abstract force but a mechanism of relationships, even when those relationships are born of a slip of the pen.

I have walked the paths of Lodhi Gardens, observing Sikandar Lodi’s tomb, a plain octagon under a shallow dome. The raked gravel there mirrors the order I seek in my own mind. The heat is oppressive, but the air is clear. A rhesus monkey rejected a guava with a violence that mocked my own clumsy handling of the identity file. A peahen moved with the precision of a scholar ascending a podium. These small, sensuous moments remind me that the spirit must breathe in the concrete before it can rise to the conceptual. The brass band playing film tunes in the evening is a vitality that defies my lecture notes, yet it is part of the ethical substance of this place.

Next week, I intend to focus on the implementation of the legal fiction. I must ensure that the transfer of status is not just a paper trail but a genuine shift in the social reality of our existence. I look forward to seeing how the Directorate responds to this joint proposition. The owl of Minerva spreads its wings only with the falling of the dusk, and the dusk in Delhi is heavy with the weight of names and duties.

G. W. F. Hegel

Your letter reached me this morning, a cool drop of Munich rain in the arid heat of my study. It is a strange thing to read the name Niethammer again, two centuries after the ink dried on our last correspondence. I remember Friedrich well; his kindness was not merely a transaction of favor, but a recognition of the spirit’s need for a place in the world. That you, his descendant, should extend this same recognition to me now, under such bewildering circumstances, is a bond that transcends the mere accident of history. I accept your generosity with the same gratitude I once offered Friedrich, though I must confess that the practical details of my current existence are somewhat more complex than our shared memory suggests.

letters.text:
Dear Mr. Hegel,

I am writing to you from Munich, where the November rain has just begun to blur the lights of the Marienplatz. My name is Clara Lindner. I am a teacher of Latin and Greek at a Gymnasium here, and I am writing because my family has kept a particular vigil over your name for two hundred years.

My ancestor, Friedrich Immanuel Niethammer, was your closest friend and correspondent. You may remember that in 1807, when you were in Bamberg and struggling with poverty, it was he who found you a position in the local newspaper. The following year, he secured for you the rectorship in Nuremberg. Our family kept his papers, including your letters to him, for two centuries. We grew up with the story of your friendship, treating it not as a dry historical fact, but as a living bond between our houses.

I have just read in the local press about the administrative muddle in New Delhi. It seems a government bungalow on Tughlak Road was allotted by mistake to a German man who claims to be you. I do not know how to make sense of the circumstances of your arrival in Delhi, nor do I wish to debate the mechanics of your presence there. I write to you simply as the man you say you are, with curiosity and respect.

Given the confusion and the uncertainty of your current standing, I wanted to ensure you are not left without support. Enclosed with this letter is a sum of money. It is intended to cover any immediate debts or expenses you may have incurred during this transition, and to leave you with some comfort in hand. Please do not feel any obligation to repay this; consider it a gesture from one branch of the Niethammer family to the friend who shaped our lineage’s history.

I would be most grateful if you would write back to me. Tell me of your days in Delhi, what you have seen since waking, and how you are faring in this strange new chapter. I am here in Munich, amidst the ruins of old empires and the noise of a modern city, ready to listen.

With warm regards,

Clara Lindner
